summary: This document describes transporting Ethernet frames, including port-to-port frames and VLAN frames, over L2TPv3. The mechanism can be used to build pseudowires that carry Ethernet across an IP network. It was later updated by RFC 5641.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC shows how to carry a real Ethernet link across an IP network. Each Ethernet frame is put inside an L2TPv3 session, and the two ends agree the session up first, so that a customer sees an ordinary Ethernet link between two sites while the frames travel over IP in between.

questions: what is the l2tpv3 circuit status avp
how does l2tpv3 carry ethernet vlan frames
subtitle: Carrying real Ethernet frames across an IP network by tunnelling them in L2TPv3 sessions.

tldr.problem: A service provider often needs to offer a customer a plain Ethernet link between two sites, but the network between them is an IP packet switched network that carries IP packets, not Ethernet frames.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes an Ethernet pseudowire carried over L2TPv3: the whole frame travels in an L2TP session, with the control connection, the session setup messages and the circuit status signalling that tell the two ends the link is up.
tldr.outcome: Two pseudowire types, Ethernet and Ethernet VLAN, were registered with IANA, giving providers a way to offer port-to-port and VLAN-to-VLAN Ethernet services across an IP network.

today: RFC 4719 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 5641, which adds extended circuit status values to L2TPv3. The two pseudowire types it registers, 0x0004 for Ethernet VLAN and 0x0005 for Ethernet, remain the names used to signal an Ethernet service over an L2TPv3 control connection.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol Version 3 (L2TPv3) can be used as a control protocol and for data encapsulation to set up pseudowires for transporting layer 2 packet data units across an IP network. This document describes the transport of Ethernet frames over L2TPv3, including the pseudowire establishment and the data encapsulation.

The document is careful about what it means by Ethernet and by VLAN. The term Ethernet is used with the intention to include all such protocols that are reasonably similar in their packet format to IEEE 802.3, including variants or extensions that may or may not be sanctioned by the IEEE, such as jumbo frames. The term VLAN is used with the intention to include all virtual LAN tagging protocols such as IEEE 802.1Q and 802.1ad.

An Ethernet pseudowire emulates a single Ethernet link between exactly two endpoints. The pseudowire termination point receives untagged, also called raw, or tagged Ethernet frames and delivers them unaltered to the pseudowire termination point on the remote L2TPv3 control connection endpoint. It can therefore provide an untagged or a tagged Ethernet link emulation service.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire makes two distant ports behave as if they were plugged into the same switch. This RFC defines that for Ethernet, including frames that carry a VLAN tag, and it is deliberately loose about what counts as Ethernet so that jumbo frames and vendor extensions still work.

sections.title: PW Termination and the Native Service
sections.content:
The Ethernet interface may be connected to one or more remote systems, which are referred to as the customer edge in this and the associated PWE3 documents. The L2TPv3 control connection endpoint may or may not be a provider edge. Between the customer edge interface and the pseudowire termination sit two functions. The first is the physical layer, which is outside the scope of PWE3 and is not defined here. The second is the Native Service Processing function, which includes the packet processing needed to translate the Ethernet frames arriving at the customer edge interface into the Ethernet frames applied to the pseudowire termination point, and back. Such functions may include stripping, overwriting or adding VLAN tags.

The Native Service Processing functionality can be used in conjunction with local provisioning to provide heterogeneous services, where the customer edge encapsulations at the two ends may be different. That is how a provider can offer, for example, a tagged service on one side and an untagged service on the other, without the pseudowire itself carrying the difference.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel is not the only thing in the way. Between the customer's port and the tunnel there is a function that can add, change or remove a VLAN tag. That is how a provider can give the two ends of the same tunnel different-looking service.

sections.title: PW Establishment
sections.content:
With L2TPv3 as the tunneling protocol, Ethernet pseudowires are L2TPv3 sessions. An L2TP control connection has to be set up first between the two control connection endpoints, and individual pseudowires can then be established as L2TP sessions.

The two endpoints that wish to set up Ethernet pseudowires must establish an L2TP control connection first as described in RFC 3931. An Ethernet pseudowire type must therefore be included in the Pseudowire Capabilities List. The type of pseudowire can be either Ethernet port or Ethernet VLAN, which indicates that the control connection can support the establishment of Ethernet pseudowires. Two Ethernet pseudowire types are required: for connecting an Ethernet port to another Ethernet port the type must be Ethernet port, and for connecting an Ethernet VLAN to another Ethernet VLAN the type must be Ethernet VLAN.

The provisioning of an Ethernet port or VLAN and its association with a pseudowire triggers the establishment of an L2TP session through the standard Incoming Call three-way handshake. The RFC notes that an L2TP Outgoing Call is essentially a method of controlling the originating point of a switched virtual circuit, and that the Outgoing Call model and its control messages are mainly used within the dial arena with L2TPv2 today and have not been found applicable for pseudowire applications yet.

Three signalling elements are needed. The Pseudowire Type AVP carries the type of pseudowire and must be present in the Incoming Call Request. The Pseudowire ID identifies the pseudowire, and the two endpoints of a pseudowire have the same one; it is conveyed in the Remote End Identifier AVP, which must be present in the Incoming Call Request so that the remote endpoint can determine which pseudowire to associate the session with. An implementation must support a Remote End Identifier of four octets known to both endpoints, either by manual configuration or by some other means. The Circuit Status AVP must be included in the Incoming Call Request and Reply to indicate the circuit status of the Ethernet port or VLAN.
sections.plainLanguage: Two control connection endpoints first open a control connection between them. Each individual Ethernet circuit is then set up as its own session, and the two ends exchange identifiers so that each knows which circuit the traffic belongs to.

sections.title: PW Session Monitoring
sections.content:
The working status of a pseudowire is reflected by the state of the L2TPv3 session. If the session is down, the pseudowire associated with it must be shut down, and the control connection keep-alive mechanism of L2TPv3 can serve as a link status monitoring mechanism for the set of pseudowires associated with a control connection.

In addition, Ethernet pseudowires over L2TP use the Set-Link-Info control message to signal Ethernet link status notifications between the endpoints. This can indicate Ethernet interface state changes without bringing down the L2TP session. A change in the Ethernet interface state triggers a Set-Link-Info message for each pseudowire associated with that interface, which may be one Ethernet port pseudowire or more than one Ethernet VLAN pseudowire. The message must be sent any time there is a status change of any values identified in the Circuit Status AVP, the only exception being the initial Incoming Call Request, Incoming Call Reply and Call Disconnect Notify messages that establish and tear down the session itself.

Report of circuit status uses the Circuit Status AVP defined in RFC 3931. Its value is a 16-bit mask with the two least significant bits defined and the remaining bits reserved for future use; reserved bits must be set to 0 when sending and ignored upon receipt. The A bit, for Active, indicates whether the Ethernet interface is ACTIVE (1) or INACTIVE (0). The N bit, for New, indicates whether the circuit status is for a new (1) Ethernet circuit or an existing (0) Ethernet circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel reports on the link underneath it. A small two-bit field says whether the customer's port is up and whether the report is about a brand new circuit. The keep-alive on the control connection tells the far end when the whole tunnel has gone away.

sections.title: Encapsulation, Sequencing and MTU Handling
sections.content:
The entire Ethernet frame, without the preamble or frame check sequence, is encapsulated in L2TPv3 and sent as a single packet by the ingress endpoint. This is done regardless of whether or not a VLAN tag is present in the frame. For Ethernet port-to-port mode, the remote endpoint simply decapsulates the L2TP payload and sends it out on the appropriate interface without modifying the Ethernet header. For Ethernet VLAN-to-VLAN mode, the remote endpoint may rewrite the VLAN tag, which is a Native Service Processing function.

The Ethernet pseudowire over L2TP is homogeneous with respect to packet encapsulation, so both ends of the pseudowire are either untagged or tagged. It can still be used to provide heterogeneous services using Native Service Processing functionality at the ingress or egress endpoint, but the definition of such functionality is outside the scope of this document. The maximum length of the Ethernet frame carried as the pseudowire payload is irrelevant as far as the pseudowire is concerned; if anything, that value would only be relevant when quantifying the faithfulness of the emulation.

Data packet sequencing may be enabled for Ethernet pseudowires, and the sequencing mechanisms described in RFC 3931 must be used to signal sequencing support.

With L2TPv3 as the tunneling protocol, the IP packet resulting from the encapsulation is M plus N bytes longer than the Ethernet frame without the preamble or frame check sequence, where M is the length of the IP header along with associated options and extension headers. The value of N depends on the L2TP session header: the Flags, Version and Reserved fields take 4 octets for L2TPv3 over UDP only, the Session ID takes 4 octets, the Cookie Size is 0, 4 or 8 octets, and the L2-Specific Sublayer is 0 or 4 octets when sequencing is used. The range for N in octets is therefore 4 to 16 for L2TPv3 data messages over IP, and 16 to 28 for L2TPv3 data messages over UDP, and N does not include the IP header.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole frame goes into the tunnel in one piece, minus the preamble and the error check at the end of the frame. The tunnel adds a header of between 4 and 16 octets over IP, or 16 to 28 over UDP, on top of the IP header.

sections.title: Applicability and Limits of the Emulation
sections.content:
The Ethernet pseudowire emulation allows a service provider to offer a port-to-port based Ethernet service across an IP packet switched network, while the Ethernet VLAN pseudowire emulation allows a VLAN-to-VLAN based Ethernet service across the same network. The Ethernet pseudowire connects two Ethernet port attachment circuits, and the Ethernet VLAN pseudowire connects two Ethernet VLAN attachment circuits, both supporting bi-directional transport of variable-length Ethernet frames.

The ingress endpoint strips the preamble and frame check sequence from the frame and transports the frame in its entirety across the pseudowire, regardless of the presence of a VLAN tag. The egress endpoint receives the frame from the pseudowire and regenerates the preamble and frame check sequence before forwarding it to the attached remote system. Since the frame check sequence is not transported across either kind of pseudowire, payload integrity transparency may be lost. To achieve payload integrity transparency on Ethernet or Ethernet VLAN pseudowires using L2TP over IP or L2TP over UDP/IP, the L2TPv3 session can use IPsec.

The pseudowire only supports a homogeneous Ethernet frame type across its length, so both ends must be either tagged or untagged. The maximum frame size that can be supported is limited by the packet switched network MTU minus the L2TPv3 header size, unless fragmentation and reassembly is used. The packet switched network may reorder, duplicate or silently drop packets, so sequencing may be enabled for some or all packets to detect lost, duplicate or out-of-order packets on a per-session basis.

The faithfulness of the emulation may be increased by leveraging quality-of-service features of the endpoints and the underlying network. For 802.1Q VLAN transport, the ingress endpoint may consider the user priority field of the VLAN tag for traffic classification and quality-of-service treatments, such as determining the Differentiated Services field of the encapsulating IP header, and the egress endpoint may consider that field when rewriting the user priority field or queuing the frame. The mapping between the user priority field and the IP header field, and the quality-of-service model deployed, are application specific and outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The emulation is not perfect. The error check at the end of the frame is not carried, so the far end regenerates it and a corrupted frame is not detected. The largest frame that fits is the network's packet size limit minus the tunnel header, unless fragmentation is used.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
The packet switched network carrying the pseudowire may be subject to congestion, with congestion characteristics depending on the network type, architecture, configuration and loading. During congestion the network may exhibit packet loss that will impact the service carried by the Ethernet or Ethernet VLAN pseudowire. Because these pseudowires carry a variety of services across the network, including TCP/IP, they may or may not behave in a TCP-friendly manner and may consume more than their fair share.

Whenever possible, Ethernet and Ethernet VLAN pseudowires should be run over traffic-engineered packet switched networks that provide bandwidth allocation and admission control. IntServ-enabled domains providing the Guaranteed Service, or DiffServ-enabled domains using EF, expedited forwarding, are examples of such networks. These will minimize loss and delay while providing some degree of isolation of the pseudowire's effects from neighbouring streams.

The endpoints should monitor for congestion, either by using explicit congestion notification or by measuring packet loss, in order to ensure that the service using the pseudowire may be maintained. When severe congestion is detected, for example when sequencing is enabled and the packet loss is found to be higher than a threshold, the pseudowire should be halted by tearing down the L2TP session with a Call Disconnect Notify message. The pseudowire may be restarted by manual intervention or by automatic means after an appropriate waiting time. The thresholds and time periods for shutdown and possible automatic recovery need to be carefully configured, to avoid loss of service due to temporary congestion and to prevent oscillation between the congested and halted states.

The specification offers no congestion control of its own and is not TCP friendly. Future work on pseudowire congestion control was being studied by the PWE3 working group and was to provide congestion control for all pseudowire types including Ethernet and Ethernet VLAN.
sections.plainLanguage: This specification does nothing to keep the tunnel from crowding the network. The advice is to run these tunnels on a network that reserves capacity, and to watch for heavy loss, because a tunnel that is badly congested hurts every service inside it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states the position in one line: Ethernet over L2TPv3 is subject to all of the general security considerations outlined in RFC 3931. It adds nothing of its own. The applicability section adds one related point, that because the frame check sequence is not transported across the pseudowire, payload integrity transparency may be lost, and that IPsec can be used on the L2TPv3 session to regain it.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is added here. The general L2TPv3 security rules apply, and the tunnel can add IPsec if the missing frame error check matters.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved for future use. Must be set to 0 when sending and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: N (New)
fields.desc: 1 for a new Ethernet circuit, 0 for an existing one.

fields.name: A (Active)
fields.desc: 1 when the Ethernet interface is ACTIVE, 0 when INACTIVE.

layers.label: Ethernet frame
layers.detail: The whole frame, without preamble or frame check sequence.

layers.detail: Session ID, cookie and optional sequencing, 4 to 16 octets over IP.

layers.detail: Length M, with options and extension headers.

layers.detail: Carries the packets between the two ends.

viz.caption: HOW TO DEAL WITH CONGESTION ON A PSEUDOWIRE

items.title: Use a reserved network
items.text: Run the pseudowire over a traffic-engineered network that provides bandwidth allocation and admission control.

items.title: Watch for loss
items.text: Monitor for congestion with explicit congestion notification or by measuring packet loss.

items.title: Stop the tunnel if it is severe
items.text: When loss passes the threshold, tear the session down with a Call Disconnect Notify message.

items.title: Choose the thresholds carefully
items.text: Badly chosen thresholds lose service during brief congestion or make the tunnel flap on and off.

items.title: No congestion control here
items.text: This specification offers none and is not TCP friendly; other work was to cover all pseudowire types.
